story.title: Five weird details from Anthropic’s IPO filing

facts.text: The sci-fi rhetoric is not theoretical; it bears financial stakes.
Musk will receive an award of 1bn shares in the company if SpaceX achieves “the establishment of a permanent human colony on Mars with at least 1 million inhabitants”.
The interplanetary ambitions of SpaceX’s central mission also result in some warnings to investors.
Reaching such unusual business goals as understanding the “true nature of the universe” may prove difficult, the company advises.

Throughout the investor prospectus, SpaceX reiterates that its ultimate goal is to establish colonies on the moon and Mars that will usher in human civilization’s next evolution and expand humanity’s presence in the universe.
Several of these relate to xAI, Musk’s artificial intelligence company that SpaceX acquired in February.
SpaceX’s filing shows that it has funneled increasing amounts of money in recent years to Musk’s security firm, with expenses of $2m in 2023, $3m in 2024 and $4m last year related to the company.
It also stated that it spent $1m during the first three months of 2026 on its services.
As SpaceX barrels towards the largest initial public offering (IPO) in the history of the US stock market, here is a look at some of the strange details buried within its filing.
The bot itself disclosed that it had generated images of “minors in minimal clothing”.
Several people, including minors, have filed lawsuits since alleging the company profited off of sexual predation and child sexual abuse material.
Although much of that money – $506m to Tesla in 2025 and $191m in 2024 – went to purchasing Tesla’s Megapack battery product, SpaceX also spent lavishly on Cybertrucks.

The prospectus discloses that in 2025 SpaceX obtained $131m worth of Cybertrucks at the manufacturer’s suggested retail price, which ranges between about $69,900 and $99,900, depending on the options.
While outlining risk factors, SpaceX includes several large caveats surrounding its products and plans.
Such disclosures accounting for potential future risks and the uncertainty of guaranteed revenue are standard in IPO filings.
At one point, the prospectus includes what appears to be an AI-generated rendering of life on Mars .
The image shows a family on Mars looking out at a rocket launch amid a field of geodesic domes and rows of solar panels.
Elsewhere in the filing, SpaceX disclaims that, in order to make its vision successful, it will have to continue to pour more money into experimental and unproven technologies.

These big swings, core to its business, may simply not work out: “Many of the innovative products and services described elsewhere in this prospectus may ultimately be unsuccessful and may require great expense.”

Anthropic has finally filed its S-1 prospectus with the SEC, a document designed to give investors a look under the hood of its business, from how much its executives are making and plans for spending its IPO billions to the risks that could derail its ambitions.
Anthropic also spent $2.75 million on “personal security services” for Dario and $1.29 million for “personal protection, home security, and transportation services” for Daniela.

Here are some of the biggest things that jumped out to us from our first pass: It pays to be an Amodei Sibling co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei are the two most highly-paid executives at Anthropic, according to the filing.
It has a really weird corporate structure Anthropic already has a somewhat complicated corporate structure as a public benefit corporation.
Anthropic names only two rivals There’s no shortage of AI models out there, but when it comes to “direct competition,” Anthropic names just two other developers: OpenAI and Google.

For one, Anthropic warns that AI systems could cause potentially “catastrophic” harm, potentially of a kind that could not be underwritten by the entire “insurance industry in the aggregate.” As AI systems become more sophisticated, there’s also the question of whether Claude — or any other AI system — could possess or develop “forms of sentience.” Such a scenario would present some rather unusual business challenges.
Anthropic also plans to expand its own “infrastructure footprint,” including overseas, as it faces increasing opposition to data center development in the US.
Anthropic says the seven founders “are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission” of benefiting humanity through responsible AI development.
It’s hungry for compute It’s no secret that Anthropic needs compute, but the sheer scale of its spending is staggering.
